title: 268. Functions, Graphs & Transformations: Domain of Rational Functions
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Domain of a Rational Function with a Linear Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain by excluding the value that makes the denominator zero.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x-5}\)?
questions.explanation: The function is defined only when the denominator is not zero. Set \(x-5=0\), which gives \(x=5\). Therefore the domain is all real numbers except \(x=5\), so option A is correct.
questions.hint: Find the value that makes the denominator zero and exclude it.

questions.concept: Domain of a Rational Function with a Linear Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain by excluding the value that makes the denominator zero.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{1}{x+4}\)?
questions.explanation: Set the denominator equal to zero: \(x+4=0\), so \(x=-4\). Therefore the domain is all real numbers except \(x=-4\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Set the denominator equal to zero and solve for \(x\).

questions.concept: Domain of a Rational Function with a Quadratic Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain by factoring the denominator and excluding its zeros.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{x+1}{x^2-9}\)?
questions.explanation: Factor the denominator: \(x^2-9=(x-3)(x+3)\). The denominator is zero when \(x=3\) or \(x=-3\). Therefore the domain is all real numbers except \(x=3\) and \(x=-3\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Factor the denominator and exclude each value that makes a factor zero.

questions.concept: Domain of a Rational Function with a Factored Quadratic Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain by factoring a quadratic denominator.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{x-2}{x^2+2x-8}\)?
questions.explanation: Factor the denominator: \(x^2+2x-8=(x+4)(x-2)\). The denominator is zero when \(x=-4\) or \(x=2\). Therefore the domain is all real numbers except \(x=-4\) and \(x=2\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Factor the denominator and set each factor equal to zero.

questions.concept: Domain of a Rational Function with an Always-Positive Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Recognize when a rational function is defined for all real numbers.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{x+3}{x^2+1}\)?
questions.explanation: The denominator is \(x^2+1\). For every real number \(x\), \(x^2\ge 0\), so \(x^2+1\ge 1>0\). The denominator is never zero. Therefore the function is defined for all real numbers, so option A is correct.
questions.hint: Check whether the denominator can ever equal zero.

questions.concept: Domain of a Rational Function with a Quadratic Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain by factoring a quadratic denominator and excluding its zeros.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{2x}{x^2-5x+6}\)?
questions.explanation: Factor the denominator: \(x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)\). The denominator is zero when \(x=2\) or \(x=3\). Therefore the domain is all real numbers except \(x=2\) and \(x=3\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Factor the denominator and exclude each zero of the denominator.

questions.concept: Domain of a Rational Function with a Difference of Squares Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain by excluding the zeros of a difference of squares denominator.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x^2-4}\)?
questions.explanation: Factor the denominator: \(x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)\). The denominator is zero when \(x=2\) or \(x=-2\). Therefore the domain is all real numbers except \(x=2\) and \(x=-2\), so option A is correct.
questions.hint: Find the zeros of the denominator, not the numerator.

questions.concept: Domain of a Rational Function with a Canceling Factor
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain of the original rational function even when a factor cancels.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{x+5}{x^2+7x+10}\)?
questions.explanation: Factor the denominator: \(x^2+7x+10=(x+5)(x+2)\). The original denominator is zero when \(x=-5\) or \(x=-2\). Even though \(x+5\) cancels with the numerator, the original function is undefined at both values. Therefore the domain is all real numbers except \(x=-5\) and \(x=-2\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Use the original denominator before canceling any common factor.

questions.concept: Domain of a Rational Function with a Cubic Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain by factoring a cubic denominator completely.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{x-1}{x^3-x}\)?
questions.explanation: Factor the denominator: \(x^3-x=x(x^2-1)=x(x-1)(x+1)\). The denominator is zero when \(x=0\), \(x=1\), or \(x=-1\). Therefore the domain is all real numbers except \(x=0\), \(x=1\), and \(x=-1\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Factor the cubic denominator completely before finding its zeros.

questions.concept: Domain of a Rational Function with a Cubic Denominator
questions.learningObjective: Determine the domain by factoring a cubic denominator completely.
questions.question: What is the domain of \(f(x)=\frac{x^2+4}{x^3-9x}\)?
questions.explanation: Factor the denominator: \(x^3-9x=x(x^2-9)=x(x-3)(x+3)\). The denominator is zero when \(x=0\), \(x=3\), or \(x=-3\). Therefore the domain is all real numbers except \(x=0\), \(x=3\), and \(x=-3\), so option B is correct.
questions.hint: Factor out \(x\) first, then factor the remaining difference of squares.
